strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 12+ diverse downstream tasks (biomarker classification, segmentation, retrieval) with fair comparisons against 11 prior CT foundation models under standardized TumorImagingBench protocols

Well-motivated technical design addressing genuine volumetric CT challenges: cubic token scaling via local-global transformer hierarchy, geometric anisotropy via anisotropic patches and 3D RoPE with jittering, noisy clinical supervision via two-stage SSL+VLA pipeline

Strong and consistent empirical results: best performance on 4/6 biomarker benchmarks (LUNA16, DLCS, NSCLC-Radiomics), competitive segmentation (87.55% AMOS-CT), substantial retrieval improvements (17.5% vs 2.9% CT-RATE Recall@5)

Thoughtful implementation with careful engineering: LLM-based text augmentation with radiologist-curated examples, data filtering using TotalSegmentator, SigLIP loss for noisy many-to-many clinical pairs, separate projection heads for DINO/iBOT objectives

Public availability and reproducibility: trained exclusively on 229,619 open-source CT scans across 8 datasets with commitment to release code, model, and training recipes; extensive supplementary material with preprocessing and hyperparameter details
Clear presentation with well-motivated design choices: local-global hierarchy cost analysis, RoPE-box jittering justification for scale robustness, masking strategy adapted for 3D spatial redundancy
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: local-global hierarchy from Swin Transformers, 3D RoPE from Primus, RoPE-box jittering from DINOv3, SSL/VLA components (DINO, iBOT, KoLeo, SigLIP) all existing techniques; contribution is primarily engineering combination rather than methodological innovation

Critical ablation studies missing: no empirical validation of anisotropic patch (16×16×8) vs isotropic, RoPE-box jittering effect, relative importance of local vs global transformers, or individual SSL component weights (1:1:0.1 DINO:iBOT:KoLeo ratio). Omitting Gram loss justified only as 'narrow operational spectrum' without evidence

Unexplained performance gap on Merlin Findings retrieval: SPECTRE achieves 55.5% Recall@1 vs Merlin's 77.6% (N=32)—substantial difference on Merlin's benchmark task lacks mechanistic explanation; only claim is that Merlin 'struggles with Impressions' which doesn't account for the gap

Data distribution bias substantially undermines 'general-purpose' claim: ~88% thoracic imaging (203,360/229,619 scans) vs ~11% abdominal; authors acknowledge weaker performance on abdominal tasks but don't quantify impact or provide rebalancing analysis

Segmentation approach has acknowledged limitations: encoder-only EoMT predicts at 1/4 resolution then upsamples, paper admits this 'can sometimes obscure small or faint lesions'; performance lags nnU-Net on LiTS (80.14% vs 81.20%), undermining general encoder quality claims

Missing computational transparency: no reporting of total training time, GPU-hours, FLOPs, reproduction cost, or carbon emissions despite 24-GPU cluster deployment; critical for reproducibility and institutional accessibility

Text encoder choice unjustified: Qwen3-0.6B selected without comparing alternatives (medical-specific encoders) or ablation showing VLA sensitivity; no analysis of how model generalizes to institutions with different terminology/reporting practices

Insufficient statistical rigor: confidence intervals shown but no formal significance tests; some improvements marginal (e.g., C4KC-KiTS differences), making it unclear which are statistically meaningful versus noise

Small dataset concerns for high-variance tasks: NSCLC-Radiogenomics and Colorectal-Liver-Metastases contain only 133-134 cases with acknowledged 'large confidence intervals' (Figure 3); SOTA claims on tiny datasets less convincing

Data split and potential contamination unclear: no specification of train-test stratification between SSL stage 1 and VLA stage 2; unclear if overlap exists that would artificially inflate stage 2 benefits

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly articulates domain-specific challenges for volumetric CT (extreme token scaling, geometric anisotropy, weak supervision) and proposes principled adaptations rather than off-the-shelf application of existing methods

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: Evaluates on three diverse downstream task families (biomarker classification on 6 datasets, semantic segmentation on 4 datasets, zero-shot retrieval on 2 datasets) with standardized protocols and fair comparison to 11 CT foundation models

Practical contribution and reproducibility: Trains exclusively on publicly available data without private datasets; commits to open-source release of code and models, supporting broad community adoption

Thorough experimental documentation: Supplementary material provides extensive details on preprocessing, hyperparameters, architectural specifications, and evaluation protocols, facilitating verification and future work
Two-stage training approach: Combining SSL (geometric consistency) with VLA (clinical semantics) is conceptually sound and shows strong cross-modal retrieval capabilities
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: 3D RoPE is from Primus; local-global attention hierarchy is not novel; DINOv3 and SigLIP are existing methods with minimal adaptation. The contribution is primarily engineering integration rather than fundamental innovation

Inconsistent empirical results: Does not achieve SOTA across benchmarks (wins on 4/6 biomarker tasks, loses on 2/6; comparable but not superior to nnU-Net on segmentation; significantly underperforms Merlin on Findings-to-Image retrieval at 55.5% vs 77.6% Recall@1). Claims of superiority are overstated given selective presentation (radar plot emphasizes favorable tasks)

Known pretraining data bias fundamentally limits generalizability: Authors acknowledge corpus is 'skewed toward thoracic imaging,' yet claim model is 'general-purpose.' This bias directly explains performance disparities between thoracic and abdominal tasks, contradicting central claims about broad applicability

Missing critical ablation studies: No ablation on (1) necessity of two-stage training, (2) local vs. global attention design, (3) impact of 3D RoPE vs. alternatives, (4) contribution of each pretraining component (DINO vs. iBOT vs. KoLeo). Only one limited segmentation ablation provided (Table 7)

Weak text encoding exploration: Uses small Qwen3-0.6B (600M parameter) model without comparing larger text encoders. Report paraphrasing strategy via Gemini introduces external dependency; impact is not ablated. For a vision-language model, this is surprising underexploration

Questionable design choices lack justification: (1) Masking ratio U(0.2, 0.7) much higher than standard U(0.1, 0.5) justified only by vague 'reduced difficulty in 3D'; (2) Omitting Gram loss justified as 'narrow CT operational spectrum' without empirical evidence; (3) Fixed 36-window design for VLA appears arbitrary; (4) Window aggregation (Eq. 5-6) combining averaged patches with [cls] token seems ad-hoc

Segmentation approach has fundamental limitations: SEoMT predicts at 1/4 resolution and upsamples—this architectural constraint inherently limits detail recovery. Authors acknowledge 'smooth outputs can sometimes obscure small or faint lesions' (Figure 6). Not a true encoder-only test since decoding/upsampling is required

Computational requirements undermine reproducibility and scalability claims: Requires 24 Blackwell GPUs (4.32 TB GPU memory cluster); substantially limits reproducibility for most researchers. No discussion of computational efficiency, inference cost, or memory requirements relative to baselines

Low absolute performance on retrieval tasks: Table 2 shows SPECTRE Recall@5=17.5% vs. random 0.3%—while 58× better than random, absolute performance is limited. Underperformance on structured text (Merlin Findings) suggests limitations in learning from well-organized clinical data

Missing statistical rigor: No significance testing between models; confidence intervals in Figure 3 overlap substantially; biomarker radar plot (Figure 1) lacks error bars. Unclear which performance differences are meaningful

strengths: Well-motivated technical design addressing genuine challenges of volumetric CT: hierarchical local-global attention elegantly manages computational complexity (O(G*m²d) linear in G), anisotropic patch embeddings encode voxel geometry, 3D RoPE with jittering ensures robustness to variable spacing

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple diverse tasks: 6 biomarker classification benchmarks with confidence intervals (Fig. 3), 4 semantic segmentation datasets, 2 text-to-image retrieval benchmarks with proper statistical reporting and fair protocol

Strong empirical results: achieves best on 4/6 biomarker tasks; competitive segmentation without decoder engineering (87.55% AMOS-CT); substantially outperforms CT-CLIP on full-scan retrieval (17.5% vs 2.9% Recall@5); consistent improvements across heterogeneous tasks

Significant reproducibility commitment: trained on open-source datasets only; code and training recipes publicly released; detailed supplementary material with hyperparameters, hardware specs, preprocessing; lowers barrier for community adoption and reproduction

Clear, well-structured presentation with adequate technical depth: problem motivation is precise, architecture design is principled and justified, experimental protocols follow best practices, limitations honestly discussed

Thoughtful data curation: 229,619 scans from diverse sources with careful filtering (e.g., removing unintended head CTs via segmentation-based outlier detection), quality preprocessing, multi-region coverage enabling general-purpose pretraining

Two-stage pretraining elegantly addresses tension between spatial precision (SSL) and semantic grounding (VLA): first stage learns geometry-aware features via DINOv3, second stage injects clinical semantics via SigLIP; well-justified for noisy medical reports

Honest discussion of limitations: acknowledges thoracic data skew, encoder-only segmentation smoothing issues, and computational requirements; proper ablation studies (Table 7) on optimization and crop size
weaknesses: Limited fundamental methodological novelty: individual components are adaptations of existing techniques (DINOv3, SigLIP, 3D RoPE); omission of Gram loss justified only by 'narrow operational spectrum' without deeper analysis; contribution is primarily in engineering integration rather than innovation

Acknowledged pretraining data bias toward thoracic imaging undermines 'general-purpose' claims: SPECTRE excels on lung tasks (LUNA16: 0.92, DLCS: 0.91 AUC) but weak on abdominal (Colorectal-Liver-Metastases: 0.62 AUC); thoracic/abdominal split not quantified in main paper Table 4

Segmentation performance not clearly SOTA: AMOS-CT 87.55% vs nnU-Net 88.87%; LiTS 80.14% vs nnU-Net ResEnc L 81.20%; acknowledged limitation that smooth encoder-only predictions 'can miss high resolution details when necessary' (p.8)

Mixed vision-language alignment results: Merlin Findings Recall@1 = 55.5% (N=32) vs Merlin 77.6% (substantial gap); advantage comes from robustness to report style variation, not superior semantic grounding to structured medical text

Substantial computational requirements limit reproducibility: 24 Blackwell GPUs (4.32TB memory) required for pretraining despite 'open-source' claims; individual labs cannot readily reproduce base model pretraining, creating practical barrier to community verification

Key architectural choices lack thorough ablation: patch size 16×16×8 justified by voxel spacing but not validated; embedding dimension 1080 described as 'balance' but not ablated; window size/count (128×128×64, G=36) have no sensitivity analysis

Text augmentation via LLM paraphrasing introduces external dependency: Google Gemini 2 Flash used for generating semantically equivalent report versions; no quantitative validation of paraphrasing quality or impact on downstream performance; potential source of hidden bias

Limited architectural analysis: window-level mean pooling (Eq. 5) not justified vs alternatives; claim that 'G≪m ensures efficiency' lacks wall-clock timing comparisons; no actual memory/throughput comparisons with competing models

Generalization testing is limited: no evaluation on out-of-distribution data or domain shift; all test sets from distributions similar to training; 'generalizable representations' claims would benefit from cross-domain evaluation

VLA stage depends on paired radiology reports (only 85,689/229,619 scans have reports): unclear how model handles missing/poor-quality reports; may not transfer well to different institutional reporting practices, limiting real-world applicability

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing genuine challenges in 3D medical imaging (token scaling, anisotropy, noisy supervision) treated as core technical problems

Principled hierarchical architecture (local ViTℓ + global ViTg) elegantly balancing expressivity and computational efficiency with thoughtful geometric encoding (anisotropic patches, 3D RoPE with jittering)

Exceptional experimental rigor with 11 foundation model comparisons across 6 biomarker benchmarks, comprehensive segmentation evaluation (6+ datasets), detailed ablations, and statistical confidence intervals
Strong open science commitment: fully reproducible with code/model release, exclusive use of public datasets, extensive hyperparameter documentation, and detailed preprocessing pipelines

Competitive empirical results achieving SOTA or near-SOTA on 4/6 biomarker tasks in zero-shot setting, substantial retrieval improvements (Recall@5: 17.5% vs 2.9% for CT-CLIP), and solid segmentation performance
Thoughtful implementation details including LLM-augmented report paraphrasing with radiologist curation, SigLIP loss selection for handling many-to-many medical labels, and careful data preprocessing
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily adapts existing methods (DINOv3, SigLIP, hierarchical transformers) without algorithmic innovation; two-stage pretraining lacks ablation justifying staged vs. joint training

Significant pretraining data imbalance with 58% from NLST (chest imaging) creating thoracic bias; acknowledged but unresolved, reflected in superior lung performance (>0.85 AUC) vs. poor abdominal results, undermining 'general-purpose' claims

Segmentation limitations undermine clinical applicability: SEoMT predicts at 1/4 resolution causing poor small-lesion performance (<10mm detection 1.53% vs 22.79% for nnU-Net), masking as 'encoder-quality probing' without addressing practical constraints
Mixed text-to-image retrieval results: outperforms CT-CLIP on CT-RATE but underperforms Merlin on structured Findings (77.6% vs 55.5% Recall@1), improvements are task-specific rather than general

Limited clinical validation: all biomarker evaluation via frozen kNN without fine-tuning benchmarks; zero-shot performance may not reflect clinical deployment; no radiologist evaluation or diagnostic accuracy assessment

Insufficient analysis of key design choices: no ablations for two-stage pretraining, patch size ratio selection, window count/size, or RoPE jittering range; masking proportion increase justified only vaguely by 'reduced difficulty in 3D'

Computational requirements not discussed: pretraining requires 24 Blackwell GPUs (high barrier for reproducibility); inference latency, memory consumption, and efficiency comparisons missing; deployment feasibility unclear

Report augmentation relies on external LLM service (Google Gemini) affecting reproducibility; clinical reports inherently noisy but no annotation quality analysis; EHR codes represented as flat comma-separated list ignoring semantic structure

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation spanning three distinct task types (biomarker classification, segmentation, text-to-image retrieval) with detailed comparisons to 11 CT foundation models, providing evidence of broad applicability

Well-articulated technical motivation addressing genuine challenges specific to volumetric CT (cubic token scaling, geometric anisotropy, weak clinical supervision) with principled architectural solutions (anisotropic patch embeddings, 3D RoPE with box-jittering)
Reproducibility commitment: pretraining exclusively on publicly available datasets (229,619 scans) with promised code release, detailed hyperparameters, and extensive supplementary materials
Thoughtful system design including LLM-based report paraphrasing to handle semantic noise in clinical supervision and ablation studies on decoder variants (Table 10) demonstrating encoder quality
Honest discussion of limitations (thoracic bias, report noise, encoder-only segmentation smoothing) that strengthens credibility and provides realistic expectations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing methods (DINOv3, SigLIP, 3D RoPE) for CT; the two-stage architecture, while well-motivated, is incremental rather than fundamentally innovative

Evaluation gaps undermine generalization claims: (1) frozen-embedding kNN protocol does not assess fine-tuning performance, a critical metric for foundation models; (2) no fine-tuning experiments comparing against baselines; (3) mixed biomarker results (wins 4/6 tasks, loses 2/6) contradict 'consistently outperforms' framing in abstract

Acknowledged practical limitations not adequately weighted in presentation: SEoMT segmentation achieves only 1-2% detection rate for lesions <10mm at standard training vs. 22.79% for nnU-Net with extended training (Table 10), severely limiting clinical utility for small structures

Dataset bias and incomplete cross-domain evaluation: pretraining skewed heavily toward chest CT (203k+ chest vs ~24k abdomen scans); while authors acknowledge stronger lung-task performance, this contradicts 'general-purpose' foundation model claim; voxel spacing robustness tested only on same-domain data (CT-RATE)

Mixed and sometimes inferior text-to-image retrieval results: on Merlin Findings (Recall@1), Merlin model (77.6%) substantially outperforms SPECTRE (55.5%), weakening multimodal alignment claims despite SigLIP pretraining

Incomplete technical justification: (1) window aggregation (Eq. 5-6) appears ad-hoc; (2) no ablation on number of windows G despite being a critical hyperparameter; (3) stage-1 loss weights (1:1:0.1) lack sensitivity analysis; (4) transition optimization between local/global transformers unclear

Evaluation fairness concerns: SPECTRE trained with 24 Blackwell GPUs (24.32TB combined memory); training resources and data volume for baseline models unclear, making direct comparison difficult; different pretraining durations and data scales not systematically controlled

Generalization and clinical validation gaps: (1) no cross-scanner/cross-protocol robustness testing beyond voxel spacing; (2) saliency maps (Fig. 4) shown qualitatively without quantitative validation; (3) no clinical utility studies or diagnostic task evaluation; (4) Computational cost not discussed (likely weeks on expensive hardware), limiting reproducibility

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation clearly identifying volumetric CT-specific challenges (token scaling, anisotropy, weak supervision) that justify technical design choices
Principled two-stage transformer architecture combining local (ViTℓ) and global (ViTg) attention to tractably handle cubic token complexity while preserving context
Comprehensive two-stage pretraining combining DINOv3-style SSL with SigLIP vision-language alignment; appropriate choice of SigLIP for noisy, many-to-many medical report relationships
Large-scale pretraining on 229,619 publicly available CT reconstructions with transparent documentation and commitment to open-source release, reducing reproduction barriers
Rigorous multi-task evaluation across biomarker classification (6 datasets, 11 models), semantic segmentation (6 datasets), and zero-shot retrieval with proper standardized protocols
Strong empirical results: best performance on 4/6 biomarker tasks, competitive segmentation without decoder engineering, substantial retrieval improvement over CT-CLIP (17.5% vs 2.9% Recall@5)
Thorough documentation with detailed preprocessing, hyperparameters, ablation studies (decoder variants, text robustness), and supporting analyses
Transparent discussion of limitations including acknowledged dataset bias toward thoracic imaging, report noise/bias, encoder-only structural limitations, and high computational requirements
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily engineering-focused adaptation of existing methods (DINO, iBOT, KoLeo, SigLIP, 3D RoPE) rather than novel architectural or objective innovations

Unresolved dataset bias: pretraining heavily skewed toward thoracic imaging (58% from NLST), explaining stronger lung-task performance; no systematic region-level analysis or mitigation strategies despite acknowledgment

Segmentation evaluation using encoder-only SEoMT approach limits practical comparisons; model trails SOTA on TotalSegmentator v2-Full (88.85% vs 89.81%); Table 10 shows substantial performance gap for small lesions (UNETR: 11.12% vs SEoMT: 1.53% detection rate)

Vision-language alignment underperforms on Merlin Findings section (55.5% Recall@1 vs Merlin 77.6%), with best performance only when combining sections; suggests difficulty with structured granular findings

Missing critical ablations: no two-stage vs end-to-end comparison, limited component importance analysis (RoPE jittering, anisotropic patches, masking rates U(0.2,0.7)), no window size sensitivity studies

Downstream evaluation limited to frozen kNN embeddings without fine-tuning results; many biomarker datasets small (<200 samples) with large confidence intervals (Fig. 3), limiting statistical strength of claims
High computational barriers to reproducibility: requires 24 Blackwell GPUs with 4.32 TB memory; no training time/cost analysis reported; infeasible for most institutions despite model release
Limited representation analysis: minimal interpretation of learned features, Figure 4 saliency maps lack systematic comparison to baselines, no analysis of failure modes or model limitations

Generalization concerns insufficiently addressed: no systematic evaluation across reconstruction kernels, dose levels, contrast protocols; clinical deployment faces substantial distribution shifts not covered by public datasets

Incomplete comparisons: some segmentation baselines (SAM-Med3D) only on subset of tasks; limited comparison with concurrent work (MedImageInsight); could better position relative to other medical foundation models
